Response: We thank the reviewer for their valuable and constructive comments. We respectfully clarify
that, while the absolute resistance change (ΔR) may appear modest, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of
our measurements is sufficient. The obtained responses are clear, stable, and highly repeatable at all
tested H₂ concentrations. Sufficient SNR ensures reliable H₂ gas detection well above the noise floor,
which is a key metric in sensing applications [1-3]. Importantly, our sensor demonstrates clear and
selective H₂ detection even at concentrations below 1%, down to 0.25%. This low-concentration
detection capability is particularly valuable for practical safety monitoring where very small hydrogen
leaks must be identified. While the absolute response at these concentrations may be lower, we highlight
that maintaining stable and reproducible detection at such low levels is a significant performance
strength of our device.
We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to the response time data and understand how the figure may
have led to some confusion. To clarify, the 1000 s noted on the time axis corresponds to the duration
for which hydrogen gas was administered in each cycle, rather than the sensor’s intrinsic response time.
The actual response time, defined as the period required to reach 90% of the total sensor signal change
(t ) following H exposure, consistently ranges from 270 to 440 seconds across all measured
90 2
concentrations (0.25 to 1%). We hope this clarification is helpful.
While we acknowledge that our sensor exhibits a somewhat slower response time compared to some of
the fastest Pd-based devices reported in the literature, we would like to emphasize that, in practical
sensing applications, parameters such as signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and selectivity are often more
critical than response speed alone. Our sensor demonstrates strong SNR and excellent selectivity under
realistic conditions, which are decisive factors for reliable gas detection in real-world environments.
Nevertheless, we recognize that further improvement in response time would enhance the applicability
of our sensor.
To address this, we decorated the Pd mesh with Pt nanoparticles to reduce the response time. Previous
studies have shown that incorporating Pt nanoparticles as a catalyst on Pd-based hydrogen sensors
improves response performance [4–6]. This is attributed to the spillover effect, wherein Pt facilitates
rapid H dissociation and delivery to the Pd surface, accelerating PdH formation and ultimately
2 x
reducing the response time. In our experiments, Pt was deposited on Pd immediately after Pd deposition
via e-beam evaporation, creating approximately 5 nm Pt nanoparticles on the Pd mesh. The Pt-decorated
Pd mesh was then transferred onto electrospun TPU fiber via WF-nTP, and H sensing was performed
2
using our established setup. As a result, the response time (t ) was reduced by about half across all
90
tested concentrations compared to the Pd-only mesh. For instance, at 1% H , the response time reduced
2
from 440 to 180 seconds. However, the overall response (R/R ) was lower than that of the Pd mesh,
consistent with previous reports, likely due to increased conduction from Pt [4, 5]. These findings
suggest that response time can be further improved by incorporating catalytic materials, though
optimization of the Pt nanoparticle content and distribution is needed.
This optimization is currently ongoing and part of our future research plans; therefore, these preliminary
results have not been included in the manuscript. We thank the reviewer for raising this important point
and hope these details help clarify our approach.
In terms of selectivity, we believe there may have been some misunderstanding regarding our sensor’s
selective performance. Our contrast gases and their concentrations were carefully selected to reflect
realistic environmental scenarios for sensor deployment, following established occupational safety and
environmental guidelines. Additionally, the parameters used in our selectivity tests both for gas type
and concentration are comparable to those commonly adopted in the literature [1–2]. This approach
demonstrates that our sensor’s selectivity assessment is relevant and scientifically robust when
benchmarked against recent studies in the field.
In summary, our manuscript provides clear evidence of reliable SNR and reproducible detection
performance at low hydrogen concentrations (down to 0.25%), a moderate but practical response time
(~400 seconds), and rigorous and application-relevant selectivity benchmarking. While sensor
performance figures such as SNR and selectivity are emphasized throughout our study, we would also
like to highlight that this work primarily demonstrates the potential and versatility of our fabrication
process, paving the way for future sensor development and optimization. We believe these
improvements and clarifications fully address the reviewer’s concerns and thank you again for your
thoughtful feedback and for giving us the opportunity to strengthen our work.
